report:
Conclusion: The claim is **supported, with nuance**. The key randomized trial found chlorhexidine–alcohol before cesarean had lower surgical-site infection than iodine–alcohol: 4.0% vs 7.3% (RR 0.55; 95% CI 0.34–0.90), with reductions in superficial and deep infections (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048). A cesarean-focused systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI versus povidone-iodine solutions, with no heterogeneity across studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/). A 2024 network meta-analysis ranked alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine highest for SSI prevention, though credible intervals overlapped, so superiority is probabilistic rather than absolute (https://www.journalofhospitalinfection.com/article/S0195-6701(24)00128-2/abstract).

Important caveat: not every trial agrees. The CAPICA randomized trial found chlorhexidine–alcohol did **not** reduce SSI versus povidone–iodine aqueous scrub/paint (6.3% vs 7.0%), but that comparator and technique differ from iodine–alcohol (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/). Overall, for the specific comparison in the claim—alcohol-based chlorhexidine versus alcohol-based iodine before cesarean—the best direct evidence favors chlorhexidine–alcohol. Formulation, alcohol content, application method, antibiotic prophylaxis, and local resistance patterns still matter.
